### CASSIODORUS of Ticino, <note>original: "Ticinensis"</note> to the most eloquent master of both languages <note>A common Renaissance compliment referring to proficiency in both Latin and Greek.</note> and most distinguished cultivator of the Muses, Lord Bernardino of Padua, <note>original: "Patavino"</note> wishes Everlasting Happiness. Dedicated.

---

Many and many days have passed, my Bernardino, since I was requested by Master Nicolo Zopino <note>Niccolò Zoppino (active 1503–1544) was a prominent Venetian printer known for publishing vernacular Italian literature.</note> to diligently review and correct the present work, so that, once corrected, he might release it once again into the light. He affirmed that much profit for him and no small praise for me would result from this endeavor. Being unable to rightfully refuse his honest request—not for the fleeting honor that I might gain from my commendable labor, but to satisfy the reasonable prayers of a friend—I took up the task (laborious though it was) to uproot the errors that had sprouted in the aforementioned work. Previously, it lay in print in a state far from well-corrected, no differently than a glittering gem lying in the vilest filth; because of this, it brought much more dishonor than praise to its excellent author. I, nevertheless, as far as the powers of my weak intellect allowed, have restored it to its original brilliance with accurate vigilance, while not neglecting the observation of the rules of the most polished vernacular <term>volgar: the Italian language as spoken and written by the people, as opposed to Latin</term> tongue. This shall be a cause of no small delight to everyone who, like you, is a follower of such refinement.

## CHAPTER ONE.

The Platonists establish as their
dogma and principal foundation that every
created thing has its being in three
ways. Although these are named differently
by various people, they nonetheless
converge upon the same meaning, and can
be named by us for now in this manner:
Causal being, Formal being, and Participated being.
This distinction cannot be expressed through
mere terms alone, but it shall be made most
manifest through an example. IN THE SUN, according
to the Philosophers <note>Referring to the Aristotelian-Scholastic view that celestial bodies were made of a "fifth element" (aether) and did not possess the "corruptible" qualities of the four earthly elements like heat or cold.</note>, there is no heat, because heat is an elemental
quality and not of a celestial nature; nevertheless, the sun is the
cause and source of all heat. Fire is hot, and it is hot
by its nature and by its own proper form.
A piece of wood is not hot by itself, but it can certainly
be heated by fire, participating <term>participando: a key Platonic concept where a lower object shares in the quality of a higher source without being that source itself.</term> in the aforementioned
quality from it. Therefore, this thing called heat, has

<meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter One regarding the three modes of being (Causal, Formal, and Participated). The previous page established these modes using the example of heat: it is "causal" in the sun, "formal" in fire, and "participated" in wood. This page applies this ontological hierarchy to the nature of God and the Divine Intellect.</meta>

BOOK ONE

in the sun it is causal. In fire it is formal. In wood, or other similar matter, it is participated. Of these three modes of being, the most noble and the most perfect is causal being; and therefore the Platonists <note>Refers to the Neoplatonic school, which emphasized a hierarchical "emanation" of reality from a single source.</note>, regarding every perfection that is granted to exist in God, wish for it to be in Him according to this mode of being. For this reason, they will say that in God there is no "thing" at all, but rather that He is the cause of all things. Similarly, they say that in God there is no intellect <note>In this context, "intellect" refers to the process of thinking or reasoning, which the Platonists viewed as a limitation because it implies a transition from one thought to another.</note>, but that He is the source and principle of every intellect. These sayings, because their foundation is not understood, give no little trouble to modern Platonists; and I recall that once a great Platonist told me he wondered much <margin>Plotinus</margin> at a saying of Plotinus <note>Plotinus (c. 204–270 AD), the primary philosopher of Neoplatonism, who taught that the ultimate source, the One, is beyond all categories of being and thought.</note>, where he says that God understands nothing nor knows anything. 

But perhaps it is more to be wondered at *how* He does not understand—that is, in what manner Plotinus intends for God not to understand. This is nothing other than his desire that this perfection of understanding should be in God according to that causal being, and not according to that formal being. <margin>In what way God understands according to Plotinus</margin> This is not to deny understanding to God, but to attribute it to Him in a more perfect and excellent way. That this is so can be clearly understood from Dionysius the Areopagite <margin>Dionysius the Areopagite</margin> <note>Pseudo-Dionysius (5th-6th century), a theologian who blended Christian doctrine with Neoplatonic philosophy. He is the "principle of Christian theologians" because his works were foundational to medieval mysticism.</note>, the prince of Christian theologians, who maintains that God knows not only Himself, but also every smallest and particular thing; yet he uses the same manner of speaking as Plotinus, saying that God is not an intellectual or intelligent nature, but is above every intellect and cognition.

<summary>Pico explains that Platonists describe God as "not knowing" or "not being" to emphasize that His existence is Causal and superior to any specific form of being or intellect. He reconciles the radical philosophy of Plotinus with the Christian mysticism of Dionysius the Areopagite.</summary>

## That all creatures are divided into three ranks.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>1. Corporeal and visible: the heavens and elements</margin>
The Platonists <note>The author refers to the Neoplatonists, such as Plotinus and Proclus, whose ideas were central to the Italian Renaissance.</note> distinguish every creature into three ranks, of which two are extremes. Under the first is included every corporeal and visible creature, such as the Heavens, the elements, plants, animals, and everything composed of the elements. Under the other is understood every invisible creature—not only incorporeal, but also entirely free and separate from any body—which is properly called <term>intellectual nature</term> <note>In this context, a "nature" consisting of pure mind or spirit, without physical form.</note>, and is called <term>Angelic nature</term> by our theologians. 

<margin>2. Intellectual nature. 3. Middle nature: Rational Soul</margin>
In the middle of these two extremes is a "middle nature," which, although it is incorporeal, invisible, and immortal, is nonetheless a mover of bodies and is bound to this service. This is called the <term>rational soul</term>. In the hierarchy of existence, it is placed below the Angelic nature and set above the corporeal; it is subject to the former and mistress of the latter. 

<margin>In what divinity consists according to the Platonists</margin>
Above these three ranks is God Himself, the author and principle of every creature. Every creature, as if from its source, possesses its <term>causal being</term> <note>The state of existing as a potential or idea within the mind of God.</note> within the divinity. Then, proceeding from Him through a middle stage into the Angelic nature, it has its second mode of being, which is <term>formal being</term>. Finally, in the rational soul, the divinity shines forth through the Angelic nature shared with it; thus the Platonists say that this divinity [is found] in three natures with...

For example <note>original: "verbigratia"</note>, the most perfect color among all colors cannot be more than one, because if there were two or more, it would necessarily follow that one of them was more or less perfect than the other; otherwise, one would be the same as the other, and thus they would not be many, but one. Therefore, that which is less perfect than the other will not be most perfect. Similarly, if God had produced another creature beyond this Mind, it would not have been most perfect, because it would have been less perfect than the first. I am accustomed to bringing forth this reasoning to confirm this opinion, and it seems to me more effective than the one used by Avicenna <margin>Avicenna</margin>, which is based on this principle: that from a cause, insofar as it is one, no more than one effect can proceed <note>Avicenna, the Persian polymath, argued for a "chain" of creation where the "One" (God) can only produce a single "One" (the First Intellect) to maintain divine simplicity.</note>. ### Here follows the second book of the most illustrious Lord Count Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <term>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola: A brilliant 15th-century Italian nobleman and philosopher who attempted to reconcile all philosophies and religions.</term> regarding the aforementioned song <note>original: "cāzona"—referring to Girolamo Benivieni’s *Canzona de Amore*, a poem about the nature of divine love which Pico is explaining in this manuscript.</note>; it states that whenever the name of the subject being proposed is ambiguous, one must first define what is signified by that name.

## CHAPTER ONE.

Plato says in many places—and after him Aristotle <term>Aristotle: The ancient Greek philosopher whose logical works were the standard textbook for reasoning in the Renaissance.</term> and universally all the schools of the Philosophers—that at the start of treating any subject, one must first establish what the name of the thing to be discussed signifies. To carry this out, they command us that whenever such a name is **equivocal** <note>original: "equiuoco"—a technical term in logic for a word that sounds the same but has several different meanings (like "bank" for a river or a building).</note>, that is, signifying various and different things, we must distinguish between those meanings and declare in which sense we primarily intend to use that name. Otherwise, every debate remains forever confused, disordered, and in vain. Indeed, the errors of those Sophists whom Plato criticizes in so many of his dialogues arose from nothing other than a failure to know this rule of distinguishing between equivocal and ambiguous terms.

<margin>
Eudemus.
</margin>

According to Eudemus <term>Eudemus: Likely Eudemus of Rhodes, a pupil of Aristotle who wrote histories of various sciences and was a key source for later philosophers.</term>, Plato was the first inventor of this rule. Therefore, anyone who sets their hand to the works of the Philosophers, and especially the Platonists, without the use of **logic**—where the aforementioned method is learned—must necessarily [deceive] both themselves and anyone else who lends their ears

<summary>Pico della Mirandola begins Book Two by arguing that all philosophical inquiry must start with clear definitions of terms to avoid the confusion typical of the Sophists. ## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Affirmation</margin>

<margin>Love, Hate</margin>
Just as the cognitive virtues <term>cognitive virtues: The faculties of the soul responsible for processing information and understanding, such as the intellect and the senses.</term> of the soul revolve around the true and the false, so the desiderative virtues <term>desiderative virtues: The faculties of the soul responsible for wanting or avoiding things, driven by the will or appetite.</term> revolve around the good and the evil. The virtue that knows assents to that which it judges to be true, and dissents from that which it judges to be false; that assent is called **affirmation** by philosophers, and that dissent is called **negation**. Similarly, the virtue of the soul that desires inclines toward that which is presented to it with the appearance of goodness, and from that which shows itself with the appearance of evil, it flees and withdraws; that inclination is called **love**, and that flight and withdrawal is called **hate**. This is the widest and most common meaning of this word "Love" that can be understood. Under this are many species which are distinguished according to the variety of "goods" toward which our desire inclines, as, for example <note>original: "uerbi gratia"—a Latin phrase meaning "for the sake of the word," used to introduce an example.</note>...

# CHAPTER VI.

<margin>What beauty may be</margin>
This word "beauty" can be understood according to a broad and common meaning, or it can be understood in its proper sense. According to the first way, whenever several different things concur in the constitution of a third thing—which arises from the proper mixing and tempering of those various elements—that grace, that **harmony**, and that **temperance** resulting from that proportionate mixture is called beauty. 

And since every created thing is composed, and is composed with as much due reason and proportion as is possible for the nature of that thing, every created thing can be called beautiful according to the aforementioned way. In this sense, beauty is nothing other than that **tempering** <note>original: "temperamento," referring to the balanced blending of qualities or parts.</note> which causes those natures—though different and varied—to nevertheless agree and harmonize together to compose a single nature. 

According to this reasoning, no "simple" <note>In philosophical terms, "simple" refers to something that is not made of parts, but is a pure, single essence.</note> thing can be beautiful; from which it follows that in **God** there is no beauty. Beauty begins after God, because **contrast** <note>original: "contrarieta"</note> begins there, without which no created thing can exist (for if there were no contrast or division, there would be only God alone). Yet this contrast and discord of different natures is not enough to constitute the **creature**, unless through proper tempering the contrast becomes united and the discord becomes concordant, which...

<summary>The author defines beauty in a broad sense as the harmony and proportion arising from the mixture of diverse parts, concluding that while all created things possess beauty through their composition, God—being perfectly simple and without parts—transcends this definition.</summary>

# That beauties, properly understood, are two: namely, corporal beauty and intelligible beauty.

## CHAPTER VIII.

Two loves: vulgar and celestial.

Since beauty exists in visible things, and since there are two sights <note>Referring to the distinction between physical eyes and the "intellectual" eye of the soul discussed in the previous chapter.</note>—one corporal and the other incorporal—there will also be two visible objects, and consequently two beauties. These are the two Venuses celebrated by Plato and by our Poet <note>Often a reference to Petrarch or Dante, whose poetry explored the bridge between earthly and divine love.</note>: namely, corporal and sensible beauty, called the **Vulgar Venus** <note>From the Latin *vulgaris*, meaning "common" or "earthly." This refers to beauty perceived by the physical senses.</note>, and the **intelligible beauty** <note>Beauty that is understood by the mind/intellect rather than seen by the eyes.</note> that exists within the **Ideas** <note>In the Platonic sense, "Ideas" are the perfect, eternal forms or patterns of all things in the divine mind.</note> themselves. This [intelligible beauty], as we demonstrated above, is the object of the intellect just as colors are the object of the [physical] sight; it is called the **Celestial Venus**. From this it follows that since Love is the **appetite** <note>Desire or natural inclination toward something.</note> for beauty, just as there are two beauties, there must also necessarily be two Loves: vulgar and celestial. Just as the former desires vulgar and sensible beauty, so the latter desires celestial and intelligible beauty. Therefore, Plato said in the *Symposium* <note>original: "Convivio." This refers to Plato's famous dialogue regarding the nature and origin of Love.</note> that for as many Venuses as there are, there must necessarily be an equal number of Loves.

It is also unfitting for material things because, although they begin from a principle, they cannot return to it; thus, [the nature of the circle] remains proper only to the mind and the soul. 

According to many other properties, however, the name "circle" is suitable for God: first, because it is the most perfect figure of all others, just as God is [the most perfect] of all things; and only to this figure of the circle can nothing be added, which demonstrates it to be absolutely perfect. ### For what reason Venus is said to rule over the three Fates.

## CHAPTER XXI.

<margin>Orpheus, Venus</margin>
It will not, therefore, be out of place to explain for what reason **Orpheus** <note>Orpheus is the legendary Greek musician and poet; the author refers here to the "Orphic Hymns," which were highly influential in Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> says that **Venus** rules over all three **Fates** <note>The Fates (Moirai) are the three goddesses who personify destiny: Clotho (the spinner), Lachesis (the allotter), and Atropos (the unturnable/cutter).</note>, which will be made manifest solely by the principles declared above.

<margin>Two worlds: one sensible, the other intelligible.</margin>
The **Platonists** posit, as we have said at other times, two worlds: this **sensible** world <term>sensible world</term> <note>The physical world we perceive through our senses.</note>, and another **intelligible** world <term>intelligible world</term> <note>The realm of pure thought and divine reality that serves as the blueprint for the physical world.</note> which is the archetype of this one. In this world, we see a vast order, and every thing linked together and mutually dependent, joining in a friendly union for the constitution of a single whole.

<margin>What Fate is.</margin>
This order, this series of causes and effects, is called **Fate** by philosophers; and since these worldly things are images of those **Ideas** of the intelligible world—dependent upon them and subject to them—it follows that the order of these [sensible] things depends upon the order of those [intelligible] things. This [higher] order is called **Providence**, just as this [lower order] is called Fate; and

<margin>What Providence is.</margin>

...of our soul; nonetheless, few men use it, for their memory, having almost turned its back to the intellect, turns its eyes and directs them toward sensible things and the care of the body. For a full understanding of this passage, it must be understood that celestial souls possess such perfection—as all the **Platonists** <term>Platonici: followers of Plato's philosophy, who believed the soul's true home is in a realm of perfect "Ideas" rather than the physical world</term> say—that they can simultaneously fulfill both of their roles. That is, they can rule and administer their bodies without being detached from the intellectual contemplation of higher things. 

These souls were represented by many poets as **two-faced Janus** <note>original: "Iano bifronte," the Roman god of gates and transitions, depicted with two faces looking toward both the past and the future.</note>, because just as he is endowed with eyes on both his front and back parts, they can simultaneously behold intelligible things and provide for sensible ones. But other, more imperfect souls, which have eyes on only one side, must necessarily turn that seeing part toward the body; consequently, the side without eyes remains facing the intellect. Thus, they remain deprived of the vision of intellectual things. 

Likewise, if they turn their eyes toward the intellect, they can no longer care for the body and must abandon its oversight. For these reasons—because these souls are forced to leave the good of the intellect to care for the body—**Divine Providence** <note>prouidentia diuina: the idea that God or a higher power actively guides the universe toward a good end</note> has bound them to fleeting and corruptible bodies. Once released from these, they may soon return to their **intellectual happiness** <term>felicità intellettuale: the supreme joy found in understanding divine truths, considered the ultimate goal of human existence</term>, provided the fault is not their own. And the other souls which are not...

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic distinction between perfect celestial souls, which can govern the physical world while maintaining divine contemplation, and human souls, which must choose between the two. The author uses the Roman god Janus as a symbol for this dual capacity of higher beings.</summary>

# SECOND [BOOK]

...[so that they are] not prevented from the good of the intellect by the care of the body, this same **Providence** <note>prouidentia: the divine guidance of the universe</note> has bound them to eternal and incorruptible bodies. From this foundation, you can derive 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

the solution to an argument by **Aristotle** in the first book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "primo dellanima" (De Anima). Aristotle argues against the Platonic view that the soul is "imprisoned" in the body, suggesting that if the body were a burden, celestial beings would be miserable.</note>, where he says that if being in the body is an evil for the soul (as **Plato** often says), it follows that the celestial souls would be more unhappy than our own, which at least sometimes are separated from the body. And you can derive another foundation: that if we assume all **demons** <term>demoni: in the Platonic sense, these are "daemons" or intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not necessarily evil entities</term> are subject to passion, we must assume they are all mortal. Therefore, the definition 

<margin>Apuleius</margin>

by **Apuleius**—namely, that demons possess a soul prone to passion but are eternal—must be understood to mean that they are eternal because their souls are eternal, but not that separation of the soul from the body does not occur in them, just as it also happens in us. Returning, then, to our subject, I say that the celestial souls—which are represented by the poets as **Janus** <note>the Roman god of beginnings and transitions, usually depicted with two faces</note>, since they are the principle of time by means of their motion—possess eyes to look upon that **Ideal beauty** in the intellect which they love continuously, and they have other eyes to look upon lower and sensible things, not to love or desire their beauty, but to communicate that beauty to them and make them participants in it. Our souls, before they are bound to the body, are in the same way like those two-faced ones; that is, they have two faces, because, as Plato says in the **Phaedrus** <note>one of Plato's dialogues that discusses the soul's journey and its "wings"</note>, every soul—and this is understood as every rational soul established in its [perfection]...

<summary>The author explains that celestial souls are uniquely able to care for physical bodies without losing their connection to divine intellect, unlike human souls. He uses the figure of Janus to illustrate how these higher souls look both toward eternal beauty and the physical world.</summary>

# BOOK
# 22

[its] nature, takes care of the entire corporeal universe. Thus, finally, our souls also—before they fall into this earthly body—likewise possess two faces, meaning that they can simultaneously look upon intellectual things and provide for sensible things. However, when they descend into the body, it happens to them just as if they were divided in half, and of the two faces only one remains to them. Because of this, whenever they turn that one remaining face toward sensible beauty, they remain deprived of the vision of the other. From this it follows that no one can possess at the same time both vulgar love and celestial love <note>vulgar love refers to the attraction to physical bodies, while celestial love refers to the soul's yearning for divine truth and the "Ideal" form of beauty</note>.

<margin>Zoroaster</margin>

And therefore **Zoroaster** <note>original: "Zoroastre." Referring to the legendary ancient Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance Neoplatonism as a source of "Chaldean" wisdom</note>, encouraging us toward the vision of that supreme beauty, exclaims: "stretch out your eyes and direct them upward." Of this, it can be well witnessed that many, by the same cause that enraptured them to the vision of intellectual beauty, have been blinded in their corporeal eyes with which sensible beauty is seen.

<margin>The Fable of Tiresias; Callimachus; Pallas</margin>

This is the meaning of the fable of **Tiresias** <note>a famous blind prophet of Thebes in Greek mythology</note> sung by **Callimachus** <note>an ancient Greek poet and scholar</note>. Tiresias, because he saw **Pallas** <note>Pallas Athena, the goddess of wisdom</note> naked—which signifies nothing other than that Ideal beauty from which all pure wisdom proceeds, and not clothed or covered by matter—suddenly became blind. By that same Pallas he was made a prophet, so that she who closed his corporeal eyes opened the eyes of his intellect, with which he could see future things no less than present ones. **Homer**, likewise, [was blinded] by the shade of **Achilles**, by whom he was inspired with that poe-

That adorns the mind, the spirit, and the body.
From here the eyes—and through the eyes to where

From here Love delights the soul, and the heart dotes upon this concept

For while it yearns for the truth,
It sees it like a ray of the Sun under water.
Yet some divine thing that flashes within it,
Though shadowed, entices the piteous heart.

<margin>Explanation of the first difference</margin>
Love FROM WHOSE HANDS THE REIN HANGS SUSPENDED, and after many verses adds: MOVES MY TONGUE AND FORCES MY GENIUS <note>original: "ingegno." In this context, it refers to the poet's creative intellect or natural talent.</note>.

This is the beginning of the present Song by our Poet <note>Referring to Girolamo Benivieni.</note>. The other, composed by Guido <note>Guido Cavalcanti (c. 1255–1300), a famous Florentine poet and friend of Dante Alighieri.</note>, begins A LADY ASKS ME BECAUSE I WISH TO SPEAK <note>original: "Donna mi prega perch'io voglia dire." This is the opening line of Cavalcanti's most famous and complex philosophical poem on the nature of love.</note>, and by its commentators it is said that by that "Lady," love is understood. In these opening lines, I note three differences between the one Poet and the other. The first is that Guido says love *asks* <note>original: "prega." Can mean to pray, entreat, or request.</note> him, and our Poet says love *forces* him. The second is that here love is called by its own proper name, which Guido did not wish to do. The third is that the former represents love as a Lady, and this one does not, but uses the customary name of "Love," which sounds like a masculine name <note>In Italian, the word for love ("Amore") is grammatically masculine, whereas "Donna" (Lady) is feminine. Pico is highlighting the different allegorical personifications used by the two poets.</note>. These differences arise neither from error on the part of either poet, nor from discordant opinions, but rather each speaks appropriately according to the nature of the love that is the subject of their poem. I said in the preceding chapter that Guido treated vulgar love, and our Poet treated celestial love. The rational soul ought not to be subjected to vulgar love, but rather should dominate it, because it is with the

[lo]cated in the lower sensitive appetite <note>The "sensitive appetite" refers to the part of the soul that deals with desires and feelings coming from the physical senses, which medieval and Renaissance philosophers placed below the "rational" part of the soul.</note> and subject to the rational part of the soul; therefore, speaking of this love, Guido says **THAT LOVE ENTREATED HIM** and did not force him. He does this to declare that the appetite of the senses cannot do violence to reason. Many people, in excuse of their vices, say that the counsel of human reason cannot resist the impetus of the sensitive part. In truth, the senses can indeed entreat reason, invite it, and entice it toward its desires; and when these desires are moderate, reason can condescend and consent to them without error. However, the senses cannot force reason in any way.

The opposite is true of celestial love. This love—being placed in the intellectual part of the soul, as we declared in the second treatise—rightly requires that the rational part, which is inferior, be subject to it. Indeed, an inferior nature never retains its freedom except when it is entirely a servant to that which is superior to it. Therefore, our Poet <note>Referring to Girolamo Benivieni, the author of the poem Pico is interpreting.</note> appropriately submits himself to the violence <margin>Solution to the second [difference]</margin> of celestial love, recognizing in this submission the greatest possible freedom.

The reason for the other difference—namely, that Guido does not call love by its proper name—is because vulgar love is not true love. Just as sensible beauty <note>Physical beauty perceived by the eyes.</note> is not true beauty, but only an image of it, so too is vulgar love merely a simulacrum <term>simulacrum: a deceptive substitute or a mere shadow of a higher reality.</term> and a shadow of celestial love. Celestial love alone properly claims and attributes to itself the most holy name of "Love." This name does not suit the other [vulgar] love in any other way than how one is accustomed to calling a statue of Her[cules]... <note>original: "Her". The text cuts off mid-word, likely intended to be "Hercule" or "Hercole" (Hercules).</note>

### *Solution to the third difference.*

## CHAPTER III.

<margin>Pausanias</margin>
The reason for the third difference—namely, that in Guido's <note>Guido Cavalcanti, a contemporary of Dante whose poems focused on the painful, physical aspects of love.</note> work, Love is signified by a feminine name, while in the work of our Poet <note>Girolamo Benivieni, whose poem Pico is currently interpreting.</note> it is signified by a masculine name—is because vulgar love stands in relation to celestial love as an imperfect thing to a perfect thing. Among the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Pythagoras; they used a table of "opposites" where the male was associated with light and perfection, and the female with darkness and imperfection.</note>, imperfect nature was signified by the female, and perfect nature by the male. 

We might also add to this that vulgar love—which concerns corporeal beauty—is more suitably directed toward women than toward men, while celestial love is the opposite. This is written in the speech of Pausanias in Plato’s *Symposium* <note>original: "Convivio." Pico refers to the famous dialogue where Athenian thinkers discuss the nature of Eros.</note>. This is because vulgar love, being a passion of the sensitive soul <note>The part of the human soul responsible for processing physical sensations and basic desires.</note>, is very prone to letting us fall headlong into the union of sexual intercourse. Since that part of the soul is more irrational than rational, when a man—overcome by his own frailty—falls into this act, it is considered less inappropriate within the female sex than in the other. 

The opposite is true of celestial love, in which there is no such danger. Instead, everything tends and is directed toward the spiritual beauty of the mind and the intellect, which is found much more perfectly in men than in women, just as with every other perfection

Socrates loved with this chaste love not only Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and general, known for his beauty and intellect, who appears in Plato's dialogues.</note>, but almost all the most ingenious and graceful among the youth of Athens. Likewise, Zeno was loved by Parmenides; Musaeus by Orpheus; Nicomachus by Theophrastus; and Clinia by Xenophon. All of these men did not desire any filthy act with their beloveds, though many believe they did—measuring the celestial thoughts of those great men by the standard of their own shameful desires. Rather, they sought only to be excited by external, bodily beauty to behold the beauty of the soul, from which the physical beauty emanated and originated. 

And since the beauty of the soul is a participation in angelic beauty, they sought to rise further up, elevating themselves to a more sublime level of contemplation until reaching the first source of all beauty, which is God. This is the fruit that Plato sought from his love, and not that shameful one which Dicaearchus <note>original: "Dicearco". A Greek philosopher and pupil of Aristotle who criticized Plato's Academy and accused Plato of being motivated by physical lust.</note> attributes to him. This was often achieved by Socrates, who, several times excited by the beauty of Phaedrus near the river Ilissus <note>A river in Athens; the setting for Plato’s dialogue *Phaedrus*, which discusses love and the soul.</note>, sang the highest mysteries of Theology.

## On the order established by divine wisdom in created things.

## CHAPTER IV. First Stanza.

*Love, from whose hands the reins hang suspended.* <note>original: "Amor dalle cui man sospes'el freno." This is likely the opening line of a poem or "stanza" being commented upon, a common structure in Renaissance philosophical treatises.</note> Among the other orders of divine wisdom established in created things, this principal one is seen: that every <term>inferior nature</term> <note>In the Great Chain of Being, an "inferior nature" refers to a life form or substance lower on the scale of spiritual and intellectual perfection.</note> is governed by the <term>superior nature</term> immediately above it. As long as it obeys that higher nature, the inferior one is defended from every evil and is led without any impediment to its determined happiness. However, if—out of an excessive love for its own liberty, and preferring a licentious life to a more useful one—it rebels against the obedience of the superior nature (just as a child might rebel against the yoke of a teacher), it falls into a double penalty. 

The first is that, like a ship abandoned by its pilot <note>original: "nochiere", referring to a helmsman or navigator</note>, it now strikes this rock, now that one, without any hope of reaching a port. The other penalty is that it loses its dominion over the other natures that were once subjected to it, just as it was once subjected to the nature from which it now rebels. To make this more manifest, we shall declare it through examples repeated from the sacred mysteries of the **Theologians** <note>In this context, "Theologians" often refers to the "Ancient Theologians" (*Prisca theologia*) such as Orpheus or Hermes Trismegistus, whom Renaissance thinkers believed prefigured Christian truths.</note>. The irrational nature is governed by the <term>providence</term> of others; due to its own imperfection, it is not fit to govern any other creature, just as God, through His ineffable excellence, provides for all things, yet He himself has no need for the providence of any other. Between...

*...to descend to us is a making of us ascend to it, because otherwise from such a union there would result imperfection in that power* <note>original: "uirtu," meaning a divine efficacy or strength.</note>, *and not perfection in the one who receives it. ...show. Regarding the second part, a doubt remains to be clarified: for what reason does our poet invoke Love and Apollo to his aid? In this matter, it should be known that for anyone who must speak on any subject, two things are necessary. First, to deeply conceive <term>conceive: In this context, the Italian "concepere" refers to the internal formation of an idea or "concept" (concetto) in the mind before it is expressed.</term> the nature of that subject; and second, to express that concept externally in an elegant manner, according to one's powers, whether by writing or by speaking. 

To achieve the first, it is necessary not only to have a good knowledge of that thing in the mind, but to transform oneself entirely into it. One will never treat a sad case well if they do not first clothe their own soul within with sadness. And if someone is to write of a martial act, such as a war that has been fought, simple knowledge of it is not enough; 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

rather, if one wishes to portray and express it with their speech, they must first compose themselves within a similar disposition <note>This reflects the Aristotelian and later Renaissance idea that for art to be "mimesis" (imitation), the artist must psychologically inhabit the state they wish to describe.</note>. So it is in every other matter. Therefore, he who has to speak of love must be transformed into 

<margin>Plato</margin>

love. For who can transform water into fire, if not fire itself? Who can transform us into love, if not Love itself? Thus, he who writes of love needs the help of Love, since he cannot write of it unless he first becomes it. 

To achieve the second, the help of him from whom the gift of eloquence can reach us is necessary; among the ancients, this was attributed 

<margin>Love, Apollo</margin>

to the Muses and to Apollo. For this reason, then, our poet invokes Apollo and Love.

Therefore, the help and benefit of Love within us cannot exist by itself in this regard without having the help of Apollo alongside it, nor can the help of Apollo in any way exist without the help of Love.

### CHAPTER VIII. Stanza 4.

->THESE, BECAUSE IN THE<-
->AMOROUS ARMS.<-

**THESE, BECAUSE IN THE AMOROUS ARMS.**
Perfect knowledge of every thing consists in understanding both its own proper nature and all its properties which follow from it. Sometimes, through properties known to us, we investigate the nature of a thing, and sometimes by the opposite process: from the knowledge of the nature in itself, we arrive at the knowledge of the properties. This latter method is the most perfect, and it is the one our Poet has followed in this place. Having declared the **nature of love** in the third stanza, he declares its **property** in the present one through that nature, and from it, he assigns the reason for the most worthy effects that love works within us.
**THESE, BECAUSE IN THE AMOROUS ARMS.** [The poet] assigns the first property...

The love which we described in the second book as being an image of **celestial love** can still dwell in one who is human, because it resides in the rational part of the soul. *Regarding this matter, it is necessary to know further that sometimes it is said that the soul is separated from the body, but not the body from the soul. This occurs when every one of the faculties of the soul—except for the one that nourishes the body, called the <term>vegetative faculty</term> <note>original: "uegetatiua"; the lowest level of the soul responsible for basic biological life like growth and nutrition.</note>—is bound and does not operate, as if it were not there at all. This, as we have said, happens when the intellectual part and "queen" of the soul is in action and at work; because of its high dignity, this part does not allow the operation of any other faculty to coexist with it, except for that of the nutritive power. The operations of the nutritive power, due to their great distance from the intellect, are not entirely nullified by its action, though they are greatly weakened. However, if the intellectual operation becomes very strong and prolonged, it becomes necessary that even with this final vegetative part, the soul separates in such a way that both it is separated from the body and the body is separated from it. ### FROM HIM DERIVES WHAT LIVES IN HIM.

Because the rational soul understands itself and other incorporeal things, it moves the corporeal things that are eternal, such as the celestial spheres, and it builds and fashions corruptible corporeal things through the motion of these eternal bodies. By moving them, as the author adds, the soul paints upon inferior matter those forms of things which it has conceived within itself. It is illuminated by these forms, which are rays of the "intelligible sun" <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for the divine source of truth and light that allows the intellect to "see" spiritual realities</note>. And just as the soul receives these forms from the Angelic Mind, so it also communicates them to matter. In this way, it spreads what it contains within itself, producing every other particular nature that exists after it. ## WHEN FIRST FORMED BY THE DIVINE FACE.

The order of the universe is that from separate and <term>intelligible: things that are understood by the mind/intellect rather than the physical senses</term> things, inferior things proceed; and these return to their causes, turning back toward them as much as they can. I see this to be wonderfully observed by the Poet in the present <term>Canzona: a traditional Italian lyric poem or song</term>. Since he must treat beauty and love, he began first with celestial beauty and celestial love—the nature, origin, and properties of which were sufficiently declared in the third and fourth stanzas. Then, having narrated in the fifth how <term>sensible: physical beauty perceived by the eyes and senses</term> beauty and the love for it proceed from that celestial source, he now shows in the rest of this poem how one ascends by orderly steps from sensible beauty to intelligible beauty. Upon reaching this, the author ends his work, as it is there—at that arrival—that every amorous desire must end. <margin>Step III</margin> The third step is when our soul—through the light of the <term>active intellect: in Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy, the faculty of the mind that translates sensory images into abstract concepts</term>—separates that received form from every particular detail and considers the proper nature of physical beauty in itself. It no longer turns to the specific image of just one body, but instead turns toward the universal beauty of all bodies together. This is the final step reached by the soul when it is turned toward the senses. For even though in this final step it regards beauty in itself, and not as if it were restricted within the "womb" of any specific matter, it nonetheless receives this knowledge from the senses and from individual <term>phantasms: mental impressions or images derived from sensory experience</term>. It is from this that a problem arises: whoever reaches the knowledge of the nature of things by this way alone cannot see them clearly and without the veil of great ambiguity. Many <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle</term>, and especially the <note>original: "latini"</note> Latins, have believed and still believe that our soul, while united with the body, cannot ascend to a more perfect knowledge. From this arises the fact that there can be two "Jovial" <note>Those influenced by the planet Jupiter.</note> people who appear dissimilar in form, because the matter at the conception of one will have been differently disposed to receive that figure of the soul than that of the other; nevertheless, what is perfect in the one is in the other like something begun but not completed.

Our Poet therefore intends that the existence of the figure of two bodies, formed by the power of one and the same star, generates between them an intense love through such conformity.

# BOOK #

<margin>
The love with which God loves within Himself
</margin>
In truth, however, there are no more than seven stanzas in the present **Song** <note>original: "Canzona"; a formal Italian poetic form</note>, although it is divided into nine parts, because none of these three stanzas is complete on its own, but one result emerges from all of them together. Therefore, the poet stops at the sixth perfect stanza, just as every lover stops at his **sixth degree** <note>referring to the final stage of the Neoplatonic ladder of love described on the previous page</note>. Being ready to proceed further, he feels Love pulling back the reins, signaling to us that for one who reaches the sixth degree, it is not permitted to travel any further. This is because that degree is the end of the amorous path, even though one may go further by way of another kind of love. That is the love with which God is loved in Himself, and not merely as the author of ideal beauty; however, that does not belong to the love of which we currently speak, because that is not a desire for beauty—which, according to the **Platonists**, is not found in God because of His **simplicity** <note>In Platonic philosophy, "simplicity" refers to being a single, indivisible essence. Since beauty often implies a harmony of different parts or proportions, these thinkers argued that God is "beyond beauty" in its worldly sense.</note>, as was declared in the first books.

### THIRD BOOK 69 ###

... [many] times, and almost always, the beloved appears to the lover far more beautiful than they are in themselves. This happens because the lover gazes upon the beloved through the image that the soul has fashioned within itself, making it so much more beautiful as it has separated that image from matter, which is the principle of all deformity. Furthermore, beyond the fact that the figure the soul has formed within itself appears much more beautiful than the external appearance—being in truth more beautiful—there is the added factor that, since this image was generated and made by the soul, the soul takes greater delight in it as its own creation. The soul even values this image more than it exists in itself and in its own proper being; and therefore the author adds:

<margin>Seventh Stanza</margin>

# GIROLAMO BENIVIENI TO
## LUCA DELLA ROBBIA.
### GREETINGS.

It was certainly enough for me once, and perhaps even rashly, that of all my verses on love, only those should appear in public

> Which, at the sweet sound of the celestial lyre,
> Singing of love, often
> Converts and draws the soul back to its first good, <note>The "first good" refers to the Platonic and Christian concept of God as the ultimate source of beauty and goodness.</note>

Without now—invited thus by your loving persuasions, and warned by the errors of my youth—having to tire the reader's mind once more with the explanation of its foolishness, that is, of my youth. Of which foolishness—truly childish foolishness, because since it pleased God to illuminate in some way the darkness of my blindness with the light of His grace—I have always considered, and still consider, the following *Bucolic* <note>original: "Buccolica." A reference to pastoral poetry, a genre featuring shepherds that Benivieni here views as a product of his immature, secular period.</note> to be no small part. Since the power to suppress it has been taken from me, I consider it more <note>The sentence continues onto the next page, but Benivieni is explaining why he is now providing a commentary or "explanation" for these early works rather than letting them circulate unguided.</note>

# ELEGY OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MI-
## randola, an outstanding youth, to Flor-
## ence, in praise of Girolamo Benivieni,
## its citizen, who himself recently as a youth
## published a Bucolic
## poem.

I REJOICE, oh Tyrrhenian <note>The Tyrrhenian Sea borders the western coast of Italy; here, "Tyrrhenian Florence" refers to the city's Etruscan roots.</note> Florence, I rejoice for you! 
Let whoever is a friend cry out "Io Paean" <note>original: "io Pean." An ancient Greek and Latin shout of triumph or a hymn of praise, originally directed to Apollo.</note> in attendance.
What honor, what fame, what glory rises for you!
Lift your head, lift your proud Libyan manes <note>original: "libycas... iubas." Likely an allusion to the lion, the "Marzocco," which is the heraldic symbol of Florence.</note>.
That man was born within your fields and your walls,
And grew up among the clear waters of the Arno <note>The river that flows through Florence.</note>.
Since there is a divine spirit in his sacred breast,
How well he takes his name from a sacred name <note>original: "de sacro nomine nomen habet." A play on the name "Girolamo" (Hieronymus), which in Greek means "Sacred Name."</note>.
He, I say, has already begun to be read everywhere with frequent applause;
He has begun to be read with honor that has no end.
His Sicilian Muse <note>original: "Sicelis... musa." A reference to pastoral or "Bucolic" poetry, a genre pioneered by the Sicilian poet Theocritus and later Virgil.</note> carries a bright, celebrated step
Through the Italian <note>original: "ausoniis." Ausonia is a poetic name for Italy.</note> cities with great praise.
Whoever reads the author envies his homeland,
And wishes for such great names for their own country.
Rejoice, rejoice again, distinguished by such great beauty,
And applaud your poet, oh blessed land.
Bind your crowned hair with vernal flowers;
Flowery wreaths befit your title <note>original: "florida serta tuo." A pun on the city's name, "Florentia" (Florence), which means "The Flowering One."</note>.
Let the crossroads be sprinkled everywhere with Persian perfume <note>original: "achemenio... costo." Costum was a costly aromatic root used in ancient perfumes, often associated with the Achaemenid (Persian) Empire.</note>,
And let many lilies be scattered through the fragrant paths.
Behold, the Benivieni line has brought into our breezes
One who, though young, bears the Tuscan face of a learned old man <note>original: "Hetruscum docto qui gerat ora senem." This suggests that although Benivieni is young, his poetry possesses the wisdom and maturity of an elder.</note>.

Lay down now, O Etruscan people, the funeral cypresses 
Which Laura gave when she was snatched by a cruel death. 
Let complaining wails be banished: behold, Laura lives again, 
She breathes and knows how to speak eloquently as before. 
Indeed, she shines more than usual, and a certain 
unknown grace of refinement comes from her face, greater than before. 
Girolamo, the pride of your city, has returned her to us, 
and has granted her the power to return from the infernal lakes <note>original: "infernos... lacus." A reference to the underworld, implying Benivieni has rescued the spirit of poetry from death, much like the myth of Orpheus and Eurydice.</note>.

she now sounds even grander with a weightier lyre <note>original: "Chely." From the Greek word for "tortoise," whose shell was used to make the first lyres.</note>.

Tuscan tongue <note>The Italian vernacular language.</note> is now equal to the Roman sound <note>The prestige of Latin.</note>. 
Yet he does not merely toss about empty, leafy winds; 
the hidden depths of his work hold more than the surface promises. 
Why should I mention how smoothly it flows, how the songs

Thus I remember often seeing sacred waters 
flow forth where no force of the rain-bearing South Wind <note>original: "nothi." The Notus was the Greek name for the stormy South Wind.</note> is felt. 
But who would wonder at such artistry in a studied poem,

<meta>This page transitions from the general dedication of the collection to the specific introduction of the first Eclogue, titled "Varo." It establishes the allegorical framework where the poet and his work are personified as shepherds seeking the patronage of Giulio Cesare da Varano.</meta>

# ARGUMENT OF THE FIRST ECLOGUE.

<margin>Melibeus</margin>
**VARO** (for so this first Eclogue is named), which, being the beginning and the head of the following **Bucolic** <term>Bucolic: From the Greek 'boukolos' (herdsman); a style of poetry focused on the lives and loves of shepherds.</term> collection, serves as a preface. It has two interlocutors: **Melibeus** and **Phileno**. Melibeus—which is interpreted as "custodian," or rather a "guardian of oxen," from which similar works are called Bucolics—represents the persona of the author. **Phileno**—which signifies "love of praise" <note>Derived from the Greek 'philos' (love) and 'ainos' (praise), reflecting the work's ambition for literary recognition.</note>—represents the present work, speaking of it as if it were a man.

<margin>Phileno</margin>
Phileno—that is, the work itself, eager and desirous of praise—seeks to transfer himself and his flocks (meaning these Eclogues) from his own paternal seat and home to that place and to that shepherd where he believes he can more abundantly, and with greater glory, achieve his desired end.

<margin>Varus</margin>
Believing that this [glory] should be found with the Illustrious Prince of Camerino, **Giulio Cesare da Varano**, from whom the Prince draws the name **Varus** <note>The title "Varo" is a classical shortening of the patron's surname, Varano, linking the contemporary lord to the Roman tradition of Virgil's patrons.</note> and bestows it upon the subject Eclogue, Phileno strives to lead both himself and those flocks of his (these Eclogues) to that place. While I carry this out, taking the opportunity to describe the City of Camerino and some of its surrounding places, I figuratively describe the glory of the Prince together with the peace, tranquility, and quiet of his subjects through rustic and pastoral concepts.

<vocab>Eclogue, Bucolic, Melibeus, Phileno, Giulio Cesare da Varano, Camerino, interlocutors</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the "Argument" or introduction to the first Eclogue. It details the internal debate of the author (Melibeus) regarding the publication of his work and introduces the transition from the literal narrative to its deeper allegorical meaning.</meta>

Interposing a resistance from **Melibeus**—that is, from me the **Author**—which is perhaps no less reasonable than it is timely and logical. I speak as one who, struggled with by the love of my own creations, wished and yet did not wish to share them with others. I wished to, invited by glory; I did not wish to, held back by fear. The former, because it arose from a poorly ordered appetite, invited me <note>The OCR reads "minuitaua," likely a transcription error for "m'invitava" (invited me), which fits the context of being 'invited by glory' mentioned in the previous sentence.</note> to publish my works. The latter, because it proceeded from sound judgment, gave me cause to think—due to the ineptitude and imperfection of the work—that in its publication I might bring upon myself infamy and slander rather than glory and honor; thus, it induced me to withhold it. 

Until finally—enticed both by the allurements and the poorly received flattery of that same vain appetite, and persuaded by the grateful memory of certain singular favors already bestowed upon me by that Prince—I at last yield. I allow her <note>The author personifies his work as a female figure or a "muse-like" entity.</note>, whatever she may be, to happily transfer herself and her flocks—that is, her **Eclogues**—to that place. There, both the obligation for past favors and the expectation of future comforts and honors envisioned there invite her.

sense
</margin>

Beneath this literal surface, because another meaning is hidden—not without **poetic dissimulation** <term>poetic dissimulation: The Renaissance literary practice of "veiling" moral or philosophical truths under fictional or allegorical stories.</term>—it shall not be burdensome for me to provide some brief notice of it as a sort of extra gesture, hinting at its intent rather than fully explaining it. According to this sense, by **Phileno** (which, as we have already said, signifies love of praise), is understood the superior part...

<meta>This page continues the allegorical "mystical sense" introduced on the previous page. Having explained the literal narrative of the author's hesitation, it now interprets the characters and setting as a struggle between the higher and lower parts of the human soul seeking divine union.</meta>

...the superior and rational part of the soul, greedy and desirous of that good which all things praise, each according to the measure of its nature—namely, of God Himself. And by **Melibeus**, the inferior and sensitive part, devoted and enslaved to the love of earthly and corruptible things. **Phileno**—that is, this superior part of the soul, thus enticed by its celestial spouse—desires to transfer itself and its flocks (meaning its powers, actions, and thoughts) from the love of these sensible things <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "sensible things" refers to objects perceived by the five senses, which were considered fleeting compared to spiritual truths.</note> and their pestilential pleasures—signified by the grass, the flowers, and the course of fleeting waters—into those ever-green and most pleasant pastures of eternal life.

<margin>Mount Sibylline</margin>
Where, near **Mount Sibylline**—a mountain truly most high, representing the counsel of God—graze the little sheep of **Varo**; that is, the elect of **Christ**, signified here by the name **Varo**, and not incongruously so. 

<margin>Varo</margin>
For this word "Varo" can, according to its root in that language in which He—that is, Christ—spoke while He lived on earth among men <note>The author refers to Hebrew or Aramaic. He likely links "Varo" to the Hebrew roots *Bara* (בָּרָא), meaning "to create," and *Bar* (בַּר), meaning "pure" or "clean."</note>, signify "creation" and "purity." It would be superfluous to discuss how well these two terms apply to Christ, who according to His divinity is most pure act and the Creator of the universe. 

**Phileno**, therefore—that is, the rational soul—desires its beatitude. # ARGUMENT OF THE SECOND ECLOGUE.

<margin>Giovanni Pico of Mirandola <note>original: "Io. pico Miran-", referring to the famous philosopher and humanist Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note></margin>
In this second Eclogue <term>Eclogue: a short pastoral poem, usually a dialogue between shepherds, modeled after the works of Virgil</term>, which is named **Daphnis** <note>Daphnis was a mythical Sicilian shepherd; here, the name is used as a poetic pseudonym for Pico della Mirandola.</note>—so called because of the excellence and dignity of that shepherd whose happy memory is celebrated within it—we intend to describe our most burning love and singular affection toward the incomparable Prince **Giovanni Pico della Mirandola**, a man truly wonderful in every respect. First, I invoke the Muses; then, their "second Apollo" <note>In Greek mythology, Apollo is the god of poetry and music. To call Pico a "second Apollo" is to elevate his intellect to divine status.</note>—that is, the Prince himself. And finally, descending to the narration of our love with moving verses, I offer a grave and tearful complaint, lamenting and accusing his already-planned departure. While I strive with every effort to call him back, myself, my flocks, my herds, and everything I own...

<summary>Meliboeus bids a final, mournful farewell to Philenus before the text introduces the second Eclogue, a tribute to the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</summary>
<keywords>Meliboeus, Philenus, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Daphnis, pastoral poetry, Muses, Apollo, fate, Renaissance humanism</keywords>

--- Page 188 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Argument" or preface to the second Eclogue, following the author's dedication to the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. It transitions from the prose introduction into the opening verses of the poem itself.</meta>

...that is, I offer him every faculty, work, and talent of mine, with a rustic and pastoral display; and finally, driven by a too-tender and impatient desire—almost as if my death must follow from his absence—I leave at the end the Epitaph <term>Epitaph: a short text honoring a deceased person, often inscribed on a tombstone</term> composed as a testimony of our love and of that unmerited and premature death of ours, to be inscribed above the front of my tomb. Through this, I tacitly exhort the reader to place their love in those things that can quiet our souls in absence as well as in presence, and which give rather than take life from those who love them rightly—and such are divine things <note>The author concludes his preface with a Neoplatonic sentiment common in the Renaissance: that while human absence causes pain, the love of "divine things" (God or eternal truths) provides constant peace.</note>.

## DAPHNIS <note>Daphnis is the poetic name used here for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note>

# ARGUMENT OF THE
# THIRD ECLOGUE.

Lauro <note>The title "Lauro" (Laurel) is an allusion to Lorenzo de’ Medici, known as "Il Magnifico." In Renaissance pastoral literature, the laurel—sacred to Apollo—symbolized both poetry and the Medici family's patronage.</note> (for this is the name of the third Eclogue, derived from its subject matter and from the excellence of that Shepherd for whom it was first composed) has two interlocutors: SYLVIO and PHILENO. Sylvio, in this place, takes on the persona of a rustic and unlearned man, a dweller of the forests—from which he derives his name <note>The name Sylvio comes from the Latin *silva*, meaning forest or woods.</note>—rather than of well-instructed and erudite cities. Phileno (which signifies "love of praise" <note>From the Greek *philos* (lover) and *ainos* (praise). This character represents the intellectual drive for fame.</note>), as we also mentioned above, signifies the character of one who is studious and desirous of glory. 

Because I estimated in my youth that the height and breadth of such glory were to be found principally in two things—namely, in the sciences (and most especially in the poetic faculty <term>poetica facolta</term>) and in arms—I depicted in this third eclogue, using a poetic style, and described the excellence, properties, and effects of poetry itself under the form of a most beautiful woman. At the end, I also touch upon something pertaining to the glory of the exercise of arms. 

By the attire, form, and beauty of this woman, I intend to suggest generally the excellence of the poetic faculty. Specifically, through her most ornate and delicate garments, I mean to suggest the admirable decoration, beautiful structure, and elaborate fictions <term>figmenti</term> <note>In this context, *figmenti* refers to the creative allegories, metaphors, and "constructed truths" that poets use to convey deeper meanings.</note> of Poets in their works. And through the lyre <term>cythara</term> and her harmonious voice, I mean to suggest the elegant...

<summary>This page serves as an introduction to the Third Eclogue, explaining the allegorical characters of the rustic Sylvio and the ambitious Phileno, and introducing the personification of Poetry as a beautiful, ornate woman.</summary>
<keywords>Lauro, Eclogue, Sylvio, Phileno, Poetry, Arms, Allegory, Renaissance Humanism</keywords>

### ARGUMENT OF THE
### FOURTH ECLOGUE.

In the beginning, this fourth Eclogue <note>An eclogue is a short pastoral poem, typically featuring shepherds and rural life as a metaphor for courtly or political themes.</note> figuratively presents and describes the most tranquil and entirely peaceful state of our city <note>Florence, Italy.</note> in the year of the Christian salvation <note>original: "Christiana salute." This refers to the year 1478 AD.</note> fourteen hundred and seventy-eight; and then the execrable storm that followed such great tranquility so poorly, together with the untimely death of GIULIANO de' Medici <note>Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478), brother of Lorenzo the Magnificent, was assassinated during High Mass in the Florence Cathedral during the Pazzi Conspiracy.</note>. Where, after having given room through piteous lamentation to the impulse of heavy sorrows—all too certain given the magnitude of such a great ruin—I finally turn to God as the first and only true cause of every good and every peace. Praying to Him that it may please Him to withdraw His hand

<summary>The page concludes a mournful pastoral dialogue and introduces the Fourth Eclogue, which contrasts the peace of Florence in early 1478 with the tragedy of the Pazzi Conspiracy and the death of Giuliano de' Medici.</summary>
<keywords>Silvio, Eclogue, Giuliano de' Medici, Christian salvation, tranquility, Pazzi Conspiracy, Florence history</keywords>

--- Page 210 ---
<meta>This page continues from the Argument of the Fourth Eclogue on page 93, concluding the prayer for divine mercy following the "great ruin" of the Pazzi Conspiracy and introducing the allegorical meanings behind the poem's title and imagery.</meta>

...of His most just punishment, and restore to us the peace and the joy of His blessed savior Christ Jesus <note>original: "Xpo Iesu." The "Xp" is a Greek-derived abbreviation for "Christ."</note>.

<margin>Nemesis</margin>
And I call this Eclogue *Nemesis*, after that power which—as poets represent in their fables—is the patroness and promoter of hatred and envy (which her name signifies <note>The author associates the Greek name Nemesis with "distribution" or "retribution," here interpreted as the source of sudden, envious changes in fortune.</note>). She is set over such hateful transformations of joyful and pleasant things into the sad and mournful. Allegorically, by the **Bull** submitting its neck to the yoke, and **Apollo** <note>Apollo here represents the Sun, and by extension, the soul or divine reason.</note> drawing away from the false waves above the horizon toward the midday, we understand the free will of man coming under the yoke of Christ. By virtue of this, the soul is raised through knowledge and love from the turbulent sea, as it were, of sensory appetites above the horizon—which is the boundary between day and night, that is, between the darkness of sin and the light of grace, and between ignorance and knowledge. It leads the soul toward midday—that is, toward the very light of divine grace and the love of its spouse <note>In Christian mysticism, the "spouse" of the soul is Christ.</note>. And by the subsequent joy, peace, and tranquility of heaven, earth, and all other created things, is signified the peace, the jubilee, and the inexpressible joy of the soul thus elevated by God through love. From this state—a truly angelic state—if the soul should fall through some sin, it is troubled in an instant, and the peace and joy of its kingdom are dissipated and overturned. Because one can quite easily understand what follows from the things already declared, it is not necessary for me to labor over a more detailed exposition.

<summary>The author explains the title of the Fourth Eclogue, "Nemesis," and provides a dense theological allegory where the movements of the Bull and Apollo represent the human soul's transition from the darkness of sin to the midday light of divine grace.</summary>
<keywords>Nemesis, Allegory, Free Will, Divine Grace, Taurus, Apollo, Christ Jesus, Pazzi Conspiracy aftermath, spiritual soul, Florence</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the allegorical interpretation of the Fourth Eclogue, "Nemesis," which began on page 93. The author is explaining how the stormy weather and mythological figures in the poem represent spiritual struggles and the eventual intervention of divine grace.</meta>

...disturbing the mind of the reader. Suffice it, then, to understand generally that by **Boreas** <note>The North Wind, traditionally associated with coldness and harshness.</note>—an impetuous wind of a cold and dry nature—are signified the temptations of the World, the Flesh, and **Satan**, which, when they are received, cool the soul's fear and love of God, and leave it arid and stripped of all spirit and devotion. By the force of the turbid and dark storm, and by the overflowing rivers, are meant the violent impulses of the senses. By the darkness of the night: the gloom of ignorance and the blindness of the intellect. By the **Nymphs**, the shepherds, and the torn and beaten flocks: every good thought, work, and affection. By **Jove** <note>The king of the gods in Roman mythology, often associated here with divine justice.</note> angry and striking with lightning: the remorse of conscience. By the ruin of the lofty tree in the high forest: the fall and the surrender of <term>free will</term> <note>The capacity of the soul to choose between good and evil.</note> in a soul that is uncultivated and fruitless. By the hill dressed in the spoils of **Bacchus** <note>The god of wine and fertility, representing the spiritual harvest.</note> and by the leaves of my salvation: **That** curdled mountain <note>A reference to Psalm 68, often interpreted in the Renaissance as the Mountain of God or the Church.</note> from which comes the wine of the **Rock** <note>original: "Petra autem est Christus." Translation: "Now the Rock is Christ." This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 10:4.</note>, and the oil from the hardest stone, and those free gifts and super-celestial illuminations and influences. Under the shadow and protection of these—like life-giving leaves—our soul can defend itself from the heat of pestiferous desires and the pleasures of the flesh, and from every other kind of temptation. And finally, by **Apollo** <note>The god of light and reason, here symbolizing the Light of God.</note> illuminating the darkness and the gloom of the sinful soul with his rays: the <term>prevenient grace</term> <note>The theological concept of grace that "comes before" human action, prompting the soul toward God.</note> and illuminating light of God.

# ARGUMENT FOR THE FIFTH
# ECLOGUE

The following eclogue laments through the personas of **Florio** and **Silvio**—that is, two pious and generous citizens. They are named generally from *Silva* <note>Latin for "forest" or "woods." The author explains that poets sometimes use "woods" as a metaphor for the "civil forest" of a city.</note>, and specifically after **Florence** <note>The original text uses "Florentia," the Latin name for the city of Florence.</note>. This following Eclogue, I say, laments through these two shepherds, with a mournful epitaph <term>epitaph: a commemorative text written in memory of a person who has died</term>, the untimely death of the youth mourned just above in the preceding Eclogue. It silently demonstrates, by the nature of his end—for which reason I call both him and this Eclogue *Atheon* <note>original: "Atheon." Derived from the Greek for "without God," here likely referring to the abandonment or the godless, cruel nature of a premature death.</note>—and by the (I know not whether to call it) variety, or rather and more accurately, the vanity of human things and affections, how foolish is he who rests his hope
Upon the world that is continually crumbling.

<summary>The narrator collapses from grief before introducing the Fifth Eclogue, which features two shepherds, Florio and Silvio, mourning a youth's untimely death. The author uses these characters to reflect on the "vanity" of earthly life and the instability of the world.</summary>
<keywords>Florio, Silvio, Florence, Eclogue, epitaph, vanity, Atheon, death, mourning</keywords>

# FIFTH ECLOGUE TITLE
## ATHEON
### INTERLOCUTORS: FLORIO
### AND SILVANO.

<margin>Florio</margin> Here is the place, Silvano, that shades and presses upon those honored limbs; here is the earth where all your old hope is buried.

<margin>Silvano</margin> Happy stone, in which pale Death locks away the one who alone holds my heart with him, and who has left me here in weeping and in conflict <note>original: "in guerra." In the poetic tradition of this era, "war" often refers to the internal turmoil and suffering caused by grief or love.</note>.
Happy stone, since heaven deems you worthy of such great honor; O fortunate place that covers and hides within you that splendor, for whom, while living, Italy—and indeed the whole world—was too small; to whom, if the truth is believed, kind Love could grant a place in heaven.
And though his body lies in this dark dwelling, perhaps from the serene heaven his spirit now looks down and sees our weeping.
Wretched am I, for I see that our condition, and every earthly good, is held under the harsh rein of death and fortune.
What shall I do, weary now? Since this single hope has been taken from me, and I see that everything the first heaven circles beneath the moon <note>The "sublunary sphere." According to the cosmology of the time, the area below the moon was the realm of the four elements and was the only part of the universe subject to change, decay, and death.</note> is unstable.
I shall weep until mercy for my heavy sufferings descends from the heavenly throne, because to change my hope would be the worst fate.
But you, mountain Fauns <term>Fauns: mythological woodland spirits, half-man and half-goat, often called upon in pastoral poetry to witness or join in a shepherd’s mourning</term>, and my sighs...

# ARGUMENT OF THE SIXTH
## ECLOGUE.

This sixth Eclogue narrates, through the persona of Cynthio <note>original: "Cynthio." An epithet for the god Apollo, often used by Renaissance poets as a pseudonym to represent their own poetic identity or the influence of divine inspiration.</note>, the most ardent love and impatient desire and affection once held within me (as is also copiously explained above in the third Eclogue) conceived from my most tender years toward poetry itself. However, the fruit I gathered from such a love was small, as testified by the things I composed and recited for her or about her at that age. I believe I was impeded partly by my natural ineptitude, and partly also by the care of many things—from which anyone who aspires to the excellence of such a practice must be entirely stripped. Whence Ovid <note>original: "Ouidio." Refers to the Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso; this sentiment echoes his writings in *Tristia*, where he argues that poetry requires a peaceful and untroubled mind.</note> rightly said that verses are the work of a mind that is vacant, free, and released from every other care and anxiety. 

The desire certainly grew in me through the heat of that age, but the labor and the aptitude were lacking. And so, continuing in the subject Eclogue and descending from one lamentation <note>original: "querimonia." A formal literary complaint or expression of grievance, typical of the pastoral genre.</note> to another, I am led to such insanity and desperation of ever being able to achieve this faculty according to the vow of my desires, that I find myself bitterly grieving over its hardness. Accusing poetry of being cruel and finally becoming enraged, I invite it to its own destruction <note>original: "interito." Meaning the ruin, death, or total cessation of his poetic efforts.</note> and common downfall. I do this out of the impatience of my desires and because of the force I exerted in learning...

He reflects on how worldly cares and a lack of natural talent prevented him from achieving poetic excellence, leading him to a state of despair.</summary>

to consider this poetic faculty, which I, along with the present eclogue, call **L A V R A** from the Laurel <note>original: "Lauro." Furthermore, by the vanity of my own goal, I wish to silently admonish the reader and exhort them to place their love there—that is, in that thing whose fruit cannot be hindered. This is especially true for those who truly seek it, hindered neither by natural ineptitude nor by any other worldly care or anxiety, as it is always open and prepared for whoever seeks, loves, and desires it with faith, simplicity of heart, and rectitude of life; and such a one is God himself.

<meta>This page transitions from the poetic verses of the previous section into an analytical commentary, likely written by Lorenzo de' Medici himself or a close contemporary, explaining the allegorical "keys" to the pastoral poems. # LORENZO DE' MEDICI.

Each one sings of their loves under various fictions and figurative concepts. Wherefore, just as in the name of Misona <note>Derived from the Greek *misos*, meaning hatred or loathing.</note>, which signifies "abomination," they figuratively condemn in their songs and exclude the inordinate love of these corruptible goods and their pestiferous pleasures; so they variously praise and commend moral virtues in the name of Floria, and supernatural and divine virtues in the name of Pleona <note>Derived from the Greek *pleon*, meaning "more" or "superabundance."</note> (which is interpreted as "superabundance"). Interspersing at times certain meanings of events that occurred in those times—in which the Turk <note>A reference to the Ottoman Empire under Mehmed the Conqueror.</note>, having already occupied the city of Otranto in Italy with part of his army—among other meanings (because it would be long and tedious to speak of them all), Floria is most particularly invited (who in that place stands for Italy) to flee with works of justice the wrath of God before the face of Polyphemus <note>In Greek mythology, a man-eating Cyclops; here used as a monstrous metaphor for the invading Ottoman forces.</note>, that is, the Turk himself. 

And exhorting her, under the name of Galatea <note>In myth, a sea-nymph pursued by Polyphemus; here she represents the Italian spirit or soul.</note>, to return through the fruit of penance and the amendment of her sins (for which she was deserving of God’s scourge) to the shade—that is, under the protection of the sacred leaves of the celestial Empire. By virtue of this protection, she might defend herself from the bites of the hungry wolves, that is, those Turks. For this purpose, Delia <note>An epithet for the goddess Diana, born on the island of Delos; here she represents Justice.</note> is ultimately invoked and prayed to—that is, Justice herself, signified here by Delia—that she might return as a remedy for this and gather herself within human hearts, as in those from which...

By this, understand our temporal possessions, which are truly but a shadow and an image of those true goods. This is evidenced by the inextinguishable thirst of those who, ensnared by the love and greed for such things, the more they abound in them, the more they always thirst for them. This is a manifest sign that they are not true goods; for if they were true goods, once possessed, they would bring peace to the soul of the one who desires them. But because they are not true goods, but only a shadow, as has been said, and an image of them, they do not have the power to quench that thirst or provide rest.
