### ARGUMENT OF THE EIGHTH
### AND FINAL
### ECLOGUE.

**Tyrrhenus** (for so this eighth and final Eclogue is named by the author, according to our native custom): here, with poetic concealment <note>original: *dissimulatione*. A common Renaissance literary technique where deeper meanings are hidden under pastoral metaphors.</note>, he gathers and describes indiscriminately certain precepts of this pastoral exercise. While he does this, not without grave and mournful lament for the ruin of my private flocks—that is, bitterly grieving for my private temporal, natural, and eternal substances <note>The author explains that the "flocks" are a metaphor for his physical health, wealth, and the state of his soul.</note>—I conclude.

## EIGHTH AND FINAL ECLOGUE

### TITLE: TYRRHENUS.

### SPEAKER: TYRRHENUS.

What fierce destiny of mine, what hard and heavy
Fate, what adverse fortune, or cruel stars,
Slow to do good, but for my harm ready and
<margin>Swift</margin> Now so afflict the wandering little sheep <note>original: *pecorelle*. In pastoral poetry, the health of the sheep reflects the internal state of the shepherd.</note>

Unhappy Tyrrhenus, who happily in so many
Toils have vainly fed your wretched heart
With a sweet deception and a wandering hope.
To what end, alas, does your sweat now profit you—

Hope—in how much error you snare the mind,

O foolish and vain thoughts; O firm and certain

Toils, [devoid] of every good and every comfort,
Of every joy and experienced sweetness.

The afflicted herds to a sweeter rest.

# GIROLAMO BENIVIENI
## TO GIOVANNI FRANCESCO
### ZEFFI. GREETINGS. <note>The original Latin "S." stands for *Salutem*, a formal greeting used in classical correspondence.</note>

My dearest Giovanni Francesco, you have urged me many times to make a copy of those things which—during the publication of my other Songs, Psalms, Chapters, and Sonnets <term>Capitoli: A verse form, usually in *terza rima*, often used in the Renaissance for moral or philosophical themes.</term> of Love (of celestial and divine love, I mean)—were set aside as not very useful. I have been somewhat hesitant as to whether I should comply with your wish. On one hand, I was drawn by your judgment and authority, by my own affection, and by the desire to satisfy you and the other friends who invited me to do the same. On the other hand, the counsel of reason held me back, for it did not seem to me that these things were worthy of being brought to light <note>original: *luce*; a common Renaissance metaphor for publication.</note>, as others judged them to be.

Yet, since it pleases you so, I think it is a lesser error to yield and be considered insufficiently cautious and prudent, than to stubbornly refuse, being too attached to my own judgment and opinion. Receive now, therefore, these neglected works of mine, certainly not as mine, but as yours. For I had once cast them out as foreign and relegated them to perpetual darkness along with many others. You, on the contrary, have not only simply received them, but with grace and honor—considering your own high standing—have approved them and restored them to the light; who could doubt that they...

<summary>In this dedication, the Florentine poet Girolamo Benivieni explains to his friend Giovanni Francesco Zeffi why he has decided to publish a collection of his earlier "neglected" poems, yielding to Zeffi's persistent encouragement.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Benivieni, Giovanni Francesco Zeffi, dedication, Renaissance poetry, celestial love, publication, Florentine humanism</keywords>

--- Page 247 ---
<meta>This page concludes the introductory letter from Girolamo Benivieni to Giovanni Francesco Zeffi and begins the first major poetic work of the collection, a poem in honor of Dante Alighieri.</meta>

...will they not now be more yours than mine? And if they are yours, as they deservedly are, and if it seems right to you and to other friends that they should appear in public, let the care, the duty, and the labor now be yours to ensure that they do so in such a way that neither you, for your honorable advice and encouragement, nor I, for my indulgence and compliance, should have cause to repent in any way. For to me, the irreparable loss of time that I once so uselessly spent in the creation and composition of these and many other similar works is already quite enough, without me now attempting, through their publication, to perhaps increase and aggravate the harm caused by the errors of my youth—a time which, given the circumstances of that age, was certainly passed with very little caution.

->Farewell. <note>original: "Vale," a standard Latin closing for a letter.</note><-

# CHAPTERS, SONGS, SONNETS AND OTHER VERSES BY GIROLAMO BENIVIENI.

## Canticle in praise of Dante Alighieri, Florentine Poet, and of his divinely composed Comedy, <note>Benivieni is referring to the *Divine Comedy*.</note> which is beyond every human concept. etc.

Already Phoebus <note>A common name for Apollo, the sun god, signifying the dawn.</note> to repair the burning wheels
Of his chariot was rising; already his lofty brow,
Already he shakes the manes of his steeds from the waves;
And already he was turning to climb the mountain,
The high tiller and the jeweled bridle

<summary>Girolamo Benivieni concludes his self-deprecating preface to Giovanni Francesco Zeffi, handing over responsibility for the publication, and begins a laudatory poem dedicated to Dante Alighieri using classical solar imagery.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Canticle in praise of Dante Alighieri." The previous page ended mid-sentence as the sun (Phoebus) began his ascent in his chariot. This page describes the speaker entering a dream-like state and discovering a beautiful landscape resembling the Earthly Paradise.</meta>

Which Phaethon <note>In Greek mythology, Phaethon was the son of the sun god who famously lost control of the sun chariot, nearly scorching the earth.</note> once knew so poorly how to guide. 
Whence from her Tithonus <note>The husband of Aurora, the goddess of the dawn.</note> the adorned daughter 
Just then rushes to the eastern slope; 
She preceded him, just as she is still vermilion, 
At the time when, far from every thought, the mind— 
As it is accustomed to penetrate the veil 
Of future things which there become present to it— <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief that dreams occurring in the early morning, just before waking, were prophetic or revealed true visions.</note> 
When, while a light sleep still veiled my eyes, 
I seemed to ascend, 
Nor do I yet know how, between the earth and the sky; 
There, as far as the eye’s arrow could turn 
All around, I see so beautiful a place 
That I thought it was the one that Eve lost. <note>A reference to the Garden of Eden, or the Earthly Paradise.</note> 
And behold, while I gaze in wonder 
At the waters, the trees, the birds, the leaves, and the grass, 
From which the adorned seat spreads out to the sky, 
My eye, which still retains the image, 
Drew toward itself a vibrant plant, 
More sharp than any other in that place. 
Beneath its sacred branches—from which Phoebus <note>The sun god Apollo, who wore a crown of laurel leaves.</note> 
Plucks his beloved garlands—a river 
Rising up irrigates the high holy land. 
The waters, beyond every natural custom, 
Shine so that on both one and the other bank, 
As they ran, they gave light without any other sun. 
Above its source, a leafy and living 
Forest crowns a dewy hill 
Which reaches as far as the river with its shores. 
There, upon the tender and soft grass

<meta>This page continues the visionary journey of the narrator, who has entered a lush, paradisiacal landscape. On the previous page, he described ascending between earth and sky to a place resembling the Garden of Eden, where a radiant plant (the laurel) grew beside a luminous river.</meta>

In the lovely hollow shaded by its branches,
The tree that Love wished to fashion from a human body <note>A reference to the myth of Daphne, who was transformed into a laurel tree to escape the god Apollo. This imagery is central to the poetry of Francesco Petrarch, who used the laurel to symbolize both his beloved Laura and his poetic ambition.</note>,
I saw, singing in the shade among lovely flowers,
A choir of ladies sitting, so graceful
That my mind is even now overwhelmed with wonder.
And from the leaves of that sacred laurel,
It seemed there rained down upon them a pleasing cloud
Of flowers, which adorned Laura, the meadow, and them alike. <note>This scene evokes Petrarch’s famous poem *Chiare, fresche et dolci acque*, where a "rain of flowers" descends upon his muse, Laura.</note>
Whence the lovely flowers, as they fell,
Covered not only the hems of their dresses
But their soft breasts, their hair, and their laps.
Above them, and around and beyond,
Hovering on their outstretched wings, one could see
New throngs of celestial loves <note>original: *celesti amori*. These are likely angelic figures or "cupids" representing divine or spiritual love.</note>.
The strange sight and the singing
Had already drawn all my mind and senses to themselves;
Wherefore, with quiet and hesitant steps,
I had already drawn so close to them
That I could somewhat distinguish in their voices
The sweet harmony that brings peace to heaven.
There, I heard (and the deep memory
Residing in my heart forbids me from keeping it silent):
“Honor the most high Poet.” <note>original: *Honorate l’altissimo Poeta.* This is a direct quotation from Dante Alighieri’s *Inferno* (Canto IV, line 80), where the phrase is used to greet the poet Virgil. By using it here, the narrator likely identifies the central figure as Dante himself.</note>
Wherefore, drawing my wandering feet ever further forward,
I came to a place where my sight
Could bear witness to their true appearance;
I saw nine ladies in a row <note>These figures likely represent the nine Muses of classical mythology, the patrons of the arts and sciences.</note>,
And in their midst, the man who through his poetry
Acquires a fame <note>original: *grido*, literally "shout" or "acclaim."</note> far above all others.

<summary>The narrator encounters a celestial gathering beneath a laurel tree, where a group of graceful ladies and angelic beings are showering flowers upon a figure identified as "the most high Poet." The scene blends the poetic imagery of Petrarch's Laura with a direct tribute to Dante Alighieri, surrounded by the nine Muses.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the speech of the "glorious Poet" (Dante Alighieri) addressed to the narrator. Having just mentioned the "fair Mount" (Purgatory), he now recounts his transition from the mountain of purification to the heavens, and explains the purpose of his famous poem, the *Divine Comedy*.</meta>

With that flesh which now no longer weighs me down. <note>original: "non mi feconda." Literally "does not fertilize me," here referring to the heavy, mortal body he left behind to become a spirit.</note>
Then he drew me onward with his comforts,
Climbing and circling the mountain <note>Mount Purgatory, where souls are purified of their sins.</note>
That straightens those whom the world made crooked;
Love, until reaching the faithful companion,
Guided us even to those clear waters
From which the beautiful mountain is nourished and bathed.
At this point my Leader <term>Duca: the Roman poet Virgil, who guided Dante through Hell and Purgatory</term> left me and fell silent;
Then Beatrice took me up, and with her
Into heaven she drew me, as it pleased Love.
Love compelled me—Love, who is always with me—
To recount what my heart saw before
In heaven, on the mountain, and down in the blind world. <note>Dante summarizes the three parts of his journey: Paradise, Purgatory, and the "blind world" of Hell.</note>
So that, having shown both one and the other way
Of heaven and of the abyss, I might be able to draw
Your hearts toward the good that every man desires.
Hence, these new celestial concepts of mine,
Love poured out into so many and so many verses,
As you well know, having read them many times.
Whence, if ever from these sacred Muses—
Who have made you worthy of their presence—
Grace was infused into your heart through me,
I pray you and desire that the ill-treated wood
Of my Lyre <note>original: "Cythara." A reference to the narrator's own poetic skill or perhaps a corrupted version of Dante's text that the narrator is meant to "retune."</note> where it is discordant
Be brought back (if it can be done) to its proper pitch.
For rarely does the sounding string
Loosen or tighten, modulating to its tone,
If the hand is guided by a deaf ear.
And here the celestial lyre fell silent.

<summary>Dante describes his ascent from Purgatory to Heaven guided by Beatrice and explains that his poetry was written to guide human hearts toward God. He concludes by asking the narrator to "retune" or correctly interpret his work, which has been poorly handled or misunderstood.</summary>

Whereupon I, with that reverence toward him
Which is inspired in a humble heart by one more worthy,
"O glory of Poets," I said, "in whom
Our language <note>original: "lingua nostra." The narrator refers to the Italian vernacular, which Dante famously championed and elevated.</note> showed how much it was capable of,
O eternal prize of the place from where I was. <note>The narrator uses the past tense "was" (fui), implying a separation from his home city.</note>
What merit or what grace reveals you to me,
Which makes me worthy to hear your word?
Who exalts me to see your glory?"
He is the glory and the first honor of this school <note>original: "scola." Likely a reference to the "noble school" of poets Dante encountered in Limbo (Inferno IV).</note>
From which issues the highest sound
That flies above every other like an eagle.
And he: "This gift is from Love and no other;
But tell me, why did you say just now 'where I was'
And not rather 'of the place where I am'?"
"Have your brothers already become as troublesome
To you as they once were to me, so that you wish
To withdraw yourself because of them from the place where you were born?" <note>Dante is asking if the narrator feels alienated from Florence due to political strife, mirroring Dante's own bitter exile.</note>
And I: "Because from this envious husk <note>original: "inuida spoglia." A poetic way of describing the mortal body which 'enviously' traps the soul.</note>
Of the mortal body, being then dissolved,
It seemed to me that I was snatched to this leaf." <note>original: "foglia." This could mean a 'leaf' of his book, or a metaphorical 'place' in the vision.</note>
"Therefore I said 'where I was'; but I see well now,
While the cause of this is being sought
By you, that I am still clothed in it." <note>The narrator realizes that despite his spiritual vision, he is still technically a living man tied to his earthly city.</note>
"The homeland which was a mother to me, but a stepmother <term>nouerca: a Latinate term for stepmother, famously used by Dante to describe Florence after his exile</term> to you,
Was and is not of such a benign style;
Now she suffers and barters her conditions,
So that her fierce Lion, <note>The Lion (the Marzocco) is the heraldic symbol of the city of Florence.</note> which used to hold
Every other in contempt, and which was so cruel and harsh
Toward us, has now become humble as a lamb."

To which both heaven and earth have set their hand
And which for many years has made you lean, <note>Dante famously wrote that the labor of his great work had made him physically thin or "lean" over the years.</note>
Has conquered the cruelty that then locked you
Out of the sheepfold, where you slept as a lamb <note>original: "ovile." A metaphor for Florence. Dante often portrayed himself as a peaceful lamb cast out by the "wolves" (his political enemies).</note>
An enemy to the wolves who made war upon it.

That God’s vengeance fears no soups. <note>original: "uendetta di Dio non teme zuppe." This is a famous reference to Dante’s *Purgatorio* (33.36). In medieval folk belief, a murderer could escape the "vendetta" of the victim's family by eating bread soaked in wine or broth (a "soup") over the victim's grave within nine days. Dante uses this to emphasize that God's justice cannot be cheated by such superstitions.</note>
Already your Lion <note>The "Lion" refers to the *Marzocco*, the heraldic lion that symbolizes the Republic of Florence.</note> inherits such a fate
That now his fleeces (and let him who wishes to hear, hear me)
He divides in his thoughts and gives them as prey.
I see him already beating his tail upon the ground;
I hear him bellow so loudly that his roar
Shall be heard from one shore of the moon to the other.
O fierce Lion, how well you are punished
For your fault; but let him who laughs at it take heed,
For the judgment of God is not finished.
For that which is given to you is for atonement
Toward greater glory; to your enemies, it shall be death
Soon enough, and let him who hears it not misunderstand.
Now because it is time that love should bring
The soul back to its nest, from whence it came here with him,
And resign it to its other companions.
Remain in peace; and as his wings
Moved to depart, such a light seemed to me
To rise from them that the eye could not endure it;
Whereupon he, the sleep, and everything vanished.

<meta>This page continues the funeral lament for Feo Belcari, a Florentine poet of religious works. It is fitting that, turned toward a greater sorrow
to give vent to its tears, the afflicted heart
now pours forth a wide river of bitter weeping.
Here one does not weep for my own personal pain,
nor for my own misfortune, nor for your deceit,
nor for your flatteries, O treacherous Love.
Shared is my <term>martyrdom</term> <note>original: "martyr". In this context, it refers to intense suffering or spiritual torment common to those mourning a great loss.</note>, shared the <term>anguish</term> <note>original: "affanno". Refers to a suffocating distress or the labored breath of grief.</note>;
shared is the grief that moves me to tears,
shared the loss, and shared the damage.
The blind world has lost that light
which, as an escort through the uncertain path for so long,
was once the servant and guide of my steps.
The celestial sound is silent; already extinguished and dead
is the <term>harmony</term> <note>original: "harmonia". This refers to the musicality of Belcari’s verse and the spiritual concord his life represented.</note> of that sweet <term>lyre</term> <note>original: "lyra". A classical symbol for the poet’s craft; here it represents Belcari’s religious poetry.</note>
which, leaving the world in affliction, now comforts heaven.
And just as his death is sighed for
here on earth, so heaven rejoices,
turning and revolving toward this new harmony.
Happy is he, who from the infected and black
valley of tears has gone to heaven, and on earth
has left only his infirm and weary garment. <note>The "garment" (uèſte) is a poetic metaphor for the physical body which the soul sheds at death.</note>
And now, released from the world and the horrible war
of vices, he <term>gazes</term> <note>original: "uagheggia". To look upon with wonder and love; used here to describe the soul's view of God.</note> upon his own splendor
in the face of Him who never errs. <note>A reference to the Beatific Vision, seeing the face of God.</note>
And if just judgment in heaven matches—
as it does—the acts and works of mortals,
he surely now shines in the most sublime choir. <note>Refers to the nine choirs of angels in the celestial hierarchy.</note>
And one must well believe that from the arrows
of the world and of fortune, his <term>Florence</term> <note>original: "Florentia". The Latin name for the city, often used in formal or poetic contexts.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the funeral lament for Feo Belcari. The previous page ended mid-sentence, describing the soul being released from the world. This page follows the soul’s ascent into the light of heaven and contrasts the eternal joy of the deceased with the "blind" grief and ignorance of those left on earth.</meta>

[May He] cover and defend [him] under his wings.
Heaven, which is gathered in a single desire and in a single
flame of love that seals its will,
unites itself entirely behind the divine pleasure;
thus it ignites and joyfully sparkles within itself
with a new <term>clarity</term> <note>original: "clarita". In Renaissance Italian, this refers to a spiritual radiance or brilliance emanating from divine truth.</note> before that [divine light],
just as a splendid spark catches fire.
And more and more beautiful because of its light,
singing <term>Glory to God in the highest</term> <note>original: "Gloria in excelsis deo". A traditional Latin liturgical hymn of praise. The poet describes the soul joining the celestial choir.</note> at every hour,
the longing new spirit gazes with love.
O life well-spent! Behold how now
you reap in heaven the eternal fruit of your well-cultivated seed,
for heaven itself falls in love with you.
Brief was his sorrow, brief was the mourning;
eternal is the reward, and such was his life
that of itself it leaves no face dry.
But what blind desire invites the lost soul
and my sad heart—woe is me—
to weep now for his very happiness?
O mind, so covered and dazzled by our <term>humanity</term> <note>original: "humanitate". Here referring to the physical limitations and mortal nature of being human which obscures spiritual vision.</note>,
that your sight
is nothing but an infirm <term>blindness</term> <note>original: "cecitate".</note>.
O blind world, o our human knowledge
full of ignorance, o proud and foolish heart,
where have you placed your goal? Where your pleasure?
It was not so that you might remain bent and turned toward the earth
along with the other beasts, o <term>wicked man</term> <note>original: "huom' iniquo".</note>,
that nature gave you a face raised toward heaven.
There is nothing under the great <term>oblique circle</term> <note>original: "cerchio obliquo". A classical astronomical reference to the zodiac or the path of the sun (the ecliptic), representing the physical universe under the heavens.</note>

<summary>The poem describes the deceased's soul entering heaven and joining the angelic choir, while rebuking the living for mourning a soul that has found eternal happiness. It contrasts human ignorance and "blindness" with the divine light and the upright posture nature gave humans to look toward the stars.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the funeral lament for the poet Feo Belcari. While the previous page critiqued the "blindness" of human grief, this page transitions into a celebration of Belcari's literary and spiritual legacy, concluding with a prayer for the soul's safe passage.</meta>

From the first heaven, so that he may flee 
the inflexible yoke of the <term>great ancient edict</term> <note>original: "grand' editto antiquo". A poetic reference to the universal law of mortality or the consequences of Original Sin.</note>.
Neither honors, nor riches, nor time or place, 
nor mortal states, nor vast empires, 
nor one's own delights or another's <term>funeral pyre</term> <note>original: "rogo". This contrasts the joys of the living with the ultimate end of all flesh.</note> 
could quiet the burning desires 
of the infirm commoners and the wandering populace, 
as one who hopes in smoke and wind.
Happy homeland, to which such sunlight 
shone from heaven through the darkness because of him, 
whence your <term>east</term> <note>original: "levante". Symbolizing both the sunrise and spiritual rebirth.</note> shines ever more brightly.
For his sacred verses and his words, 
which have already written so many pages 
of <term>Jerusalem</term> <note>original: "Hierusalem". Refers to Belcari’s famous religious plays (sacre rappresentazioni) and poems concerning the Holy City and biblical history.</note> and of the eternal offspring.
Like rays of love that shoot out 
from every gate around your sweet orient, 
they have already spread their flames through all that heaven holds.
But you, gentle spirit, who now gazes 
happily into that Mind, and into those beautiful eternal eyes 
to which all things are present,
you mirror yourself in them and internalize yourself so much 
that you see and discern in them my afflicted heart 
and its desire, however much I try to hide it.
If pity for my <term>suffering</term> <note>original: "martyro". In this context, it refers to the narrator's deep emotional anguish and mourning rather than literal martyrdom.</note> has a place in you, 
may it please you, O <term>Pheo</term> <note>A Latinized variant of the name Feo (Belcari).</note>, to pray for your faithful friend 
to Him in whom I live, and to whom I aspire while living.
So that in this turbulent and cruel 
course of such a great sea, I may safely 
withdraw my already dried sails into port.

### CONSOLATION to Messer Ugolino Verini on the death of his son, Michele.
<note>Ugolino Verini (1438–1516) was a prominent Florentine poet. His son Michele was a brilliant young scholar who died in 1487 at the age of 18. Legend at the time claimed Michele died because his doctors advised him that his extreme dedication to chastity was making him ill, yet he refused to break his moral vows.</note>

What ungrateful virtue, what impious fate, what harsh restraint, what blind, inept, and foolish fury, what new law, iniquitous and cruel, shall ensure that the immortal fountain—which bitter death has gathered around the heart in a pool of sharp weeping—is restrained and closed by its own hands?

Be silent, cruel tongue, rustic and stripped of all pity—cruel indeed! Or rather, you shall provide the harmony for his just laments by weeping along with him. Why, oh why, do your heavy, grieving sighs not open the path to your weary heart? And why, Father, in the midst of such sorrow, do you now deny your eyes the weeping they desire?

Break now that harsh restraint; despise that iniquitous law <note>The poet encourages the father to break the "law" of Stoic composure and allow himself to cry, arguing that such a great loss cannot be governed by moderation.</note> which is not fitting for your sorrow; for no limit can be set that might turn your grief aside.

### Apology to the same man

That pity which gives life to my heavy sighs
Coming from your hellish and sad soul,
Moves the compassionate heart; it awakens the lost soul
While it sometimes rouses from sluggish sleep.
That pity shapes the intellect, the heart shapes the tongue,
And the voice gives it form and then invites it out;
Once moved, it arrives partway, where—hindered
By weeping—it stops in vain in the middle of its course.
From this, the first desire moves the hand, and the hand
Then forces the pen; but what the heart
Dictates, neither the heart knows well, nor does the pen understand.
Therefore, if this mournful style, while it speaks
With you, declines and falls from its usual worth,
Let my own grief—not just yours—be its excuse.

Open your eyes now, and along the path that he 
Showed you on earth as he returned to heaven, 
Put an end to your weeping, and rejoice in his blessedness.

Was vain, weak, and slow;
Thus I lived secure in my freedom,
All too satisfied and content with my first love.

### To the same Lord. <note>Addressing Lorenzo de' Medici.</note>

### To the same Lord Count. <note>The "Lord Count" likely refers to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous philosopher and close friend of the poet Girolamo Benivieni.</note>

I have prayed and still I pray to Love, that he might entreat

because of that which binds one soul into two bodies <note>A classic Neoplatonic expression of perfect friendship: "one soul in two bodies."</note>
and which rests and lies in a noble heart;
at least let your ancient wisdom give way
to this hard, cruel, and biting fate,
which seems to weave more snares every day
so as never to have truce or peace with you.
But if you now remember well your Muse,
[knowing] that every mortal thing passes in an instant
and that we are nothing else but shadow and dust; <note>A reference to the Latin phrase *pulvis et umbra sumus* from Horace's Odes, emphasizing human mortality.</note>
you will see clearly that what is in us—which disagrees with this—
is fragile and fleeting, while its contrary is taken up
by Him who turns the universe. <note>Domenico is offering a philosophical consolation: while physical bodies and earthly circumstances are fleeting ("dust"), the divine or spiritual element within us is eternal.</note>

->Reply in the same rhymes.<- <note>A traditional poetic challenge where the second poet responds using the exact same rhyme endings as the first poem to show technical skill and thematic unity.</note>

Until the soul is divided from the wretched body
by that madness which undoes me,
there shall be no one on earth joined with me
who does not experience the fire of my torch. <note>The author responds by emphasizing the intensity of his emotional state—a "madness" or "furor" that burns like a torch, suggesting that anyone close to him must also feel the heat of his passion or suffering.</note>

These are deceptive, and those arrows are burning.

<meta>This page continues from a general lamentation on the corruption of love. The previous page ended mid-sentence describing a world in moral reversal: "But everything in the [world is turned upside down]." We now transition into a specific poetic exchange between two Florentine humanists, Bartolomeo Fonzio and Girolamo Benivieni, exploring the themes of spiritual redemption and the struggle between the rational soul and animal desires.</meta>

### Bartolomeo Fonzio to Girolamo Benivieni.

With three different arrows and a three-stringed bow,
Of which pleasure, reason, and spirit are the authors,
Girolamo, you had pierced my heart,
Which was burdened with vain thoughts and misery.
Now let thanks be given to God, who was never stingy
In lifting up those who weep for their errors;
I shed sweet tears for true love,
Thinking only of my final passage <note>original: *ultimo varco*. This refers to the transition from life to death, or the crossing into the spiritual realm.</note>.
And when it happens that the animal <note>In the Neoplatonic philosophy of the time, the "animal" refers to the lower, sensory part of the human soul which is driven by instincts and physical desires.</note> seizes
Its beautiful rational consort,
Against whose flatteries it defends itself poorly,
The <term>pious synteresis</term> <note>Synteresis is a technical term in medieval and Renaissance theology referring to the innate spark of conscience or the preserved fragment of divine reason in the soul that remains untainted by sin.</note>, constant and strong,
Ignites entirely with vital spirit;
Then it commands, and rescues me from death.

### Response by Girolamo Benivieni using the same rhymes.

If you are, from the arrows by which I am pierced,
Passing from hour to hour and from this to that sorrow,
Lightened and unburdened solely by the grace
Of that Lord who created you,
Give Him thanks; my heart—which, outside the park
Of the other beasts of the earth <note>The "park" or "enclosure" refers to the material world where humans live like animals if they follow only their senses.</note>,
Lives in its own fold with your fervor—
Bring it back, while He is yet unsparing toward my errors.
Because whenever the animal runs into the snares
That are stretched out for it, through false and 
Twisted paths, it leads itself to an end it does not intend.

### Bartolomeo Fonzio to Girolamo Benivieni.

O poet <note>original: *uate* (vates). A term for a divinely inspired poet-prophet.</note> rich with honorable gifts,
If in this life full of misery
You are not drawn to heaven by its chain <note>A reference to the "Golden Chain of Homer" or the Neoplatonic Great Chain of Being, symbolizing the divine attraction that pulls the soul upward.</note>,
It is not because the paths are unknown to you.
But if a high mortal man cannot ascend
By means of great intellect and the kind Muse <note>original: *camena*. A Latin term for the Muses, specifically associated with Roman poetry.</note>,
Hope, faith, and charity lead us there,
With chaste fasts <note>original: *ieiun*. From the Latin *ieiunium*, meaning ritual fasting.</note> and devout prayers.
Wherefore I, with a humble and contrite heart, often
Wetting my face with tears and beating my breast,
Gauge the worth of human glory and fallacious love.
For that which he who abandons himself for God
Tastes, the intellect—which is held captive by the glory
And the love of the world—does not allow one to taste.

### Response by Girolamo Benivieni using the same rhymes.

What does it profit to run upon the high seas
Along the path of the wheels <note>This likely refers to the "wheels" of the celestial spheres or the tracks/wake left by a ship following a predetermined course.</note> toward a fertile and pleasant place,
If the poorly-steered vessel, to my greater sorrow,
Sometimes strikes this rock or that?

Which hell, heaven, and the world honor.

# HOW THE MADNESS OF JESUS
### can be, and truly is, wise.

*I want to tell you, my soul,*
*Since you wish to know it,*
*But let it remain between us,*
*How madness is wise.* <note>The author uses the term *pacia*, an archaic variant of *pazzia* (madness), to describe a state of mystical ecstasy that appears foolish to the world but is spiritually enlightened.</note>

*If it is true, because it is true,*
*That the heart which rests in God*
*Has, above every desire,*
*All other things together with Him,*

*If then his own flesh is heavy and tedious,*
*And he is displeased by*
*Whatever disturbs his peace,*
*He is wise in the lap of madness.*

->I want to tell you.<-

*He who does not allow wealth,*
*Pleasure, fame, glory, or honors*
*To pull, with their sweetness,*
*Our human hearts so much to themselves*

## HYMN TO THE ANGEL
## HIS GUARDIAN.

Spirit of heaven, chosen
By God through love alone
For my protection, govern—
I pray you—my heart, body, and intellect <note>In this context, "intellect" refers to the rational part of the soul, which the poet asks the angel to guide toward divine truth.</note>.
O love, for whom another name
I do not know by which to call you,
Thinking how much and in what way
You follow, teach, guide, embrace, and love me;
Grant that I may yearn, through you,
For that Good alone, and desire the place
To which you now draw me,
Such that every other pleasure becomes distasteful to me.
->*Spirit of heaven.*<- <note>This centered line indicates a refrain to be repeated by a choir or the faithful during the singing of the hymn.</note>
Immortal eye that sees
With how many snares and traps,
And wicked, fleeing feet,
The flesh and the blind world entangle the heart;
I pray your mercy may untie and undo
That knot
Wherewith, while weaving, I bind
Always—alas—one flaw to another <note>The "knot" is a common metaphor for the habitual nature of sin, where one bad choice leads to another, creating a web that the soul cannot escape without divine help.</note>.
->*Spirit of heaven.*<-
Defend me, O kind
Spirit, from as many evils
As the malignant demon
Prepares every hour—alas—for wretched mortals.

<meta>This page continues the dedication or introductory letter from Girolamo Benivieni to Bernardo Gondi. The previous page ended with a formal greeting, and this page begins the main philosophical and theological argument of the work.</meta>

In His infinite goodness, He created this universe so that He, who could not be seen, might show Himself to our eyes under the veil of His creatures <note>In the Renaissance context, "creatures" refers to all created things in the universe, including inanimate objects and stars, which were thought to reflect God's divine nature.</note>. And thus, that which by its nature is invisible has, through what was made visible by Him, become in some way possible to see, know, and enjoy. There are three invisible things of God: power, wisdom, and benevolence <note>original: "potentia, la sapientia, la benignità." This triad is central to the Neoplatonic Christian theology of the period, often associated with the Trinity.</note>. And just as all creatures proceed from these three things, so in these three are they preserved, and by these three are they ruled and governed. 

Power creates, wisdom governs, and benevolence preserves. Just as these three things are one in God in an ineffable <note>ineffable: something too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words.</note> way, so they cannot be separated from one another in their operations in any way. Power appears through the immensity and greatness of created things; wisdom through their utility and beauty; benevolence through the useful comfort and necessity of them. 

Speaking of these things together not many days ago, you asked me—as you know—that I might be content to translate <note>original: "redurre," meaning to bring back or adapt into a different form, in this case, poetry.</note>, when I could do so at my convenience, some part of such reasonings into verse. I believe this was perhaps to accompany the utility of the discussed matters with the sweetness and gentleness of them—that is, of my verses—if, however, sweetness and gentleness can spring from them, from my naturally rough and uncultured pen. This task, though for many reasons—but especially because of the quality and greatness of the subject matter—seemed to me beyond my strength and quite foreign to the purpose of my present profession <note>Benivieni is likely referring to his later life as a religious penitent and follower of the reformer Girolamo Savonarola, which made him hesitant to engage in "secular" poetic pursuits.</note>, did not...

## THE ADMONITION OF MAN
*To the soul, through which he demonstrates how she can, by means of created things <note>The "creatures" or "created things" refers to the physical world and living beings, which in Renaissance philosophy were seen as a ladder or mirror reflecting the beauty and power of God.</note>, know and consequently love her Creator.*

### MAN SPEAKS.

What do you seek, my soul? What do you want? What do you ask?
<margin>dis[course]</margin> After so much toil, peace and rest.
You will never have peace if you do not believe in God,
If you do not hope in Him; if from this hateful
Prison of the world <note>The "prison of the world" is a classic Neoplatonic and Christian metaphor suggesting that the physical body and the material world restrict the divine soul from its true home in heaven.</note>, where for a time you dwell in tears,
You do not return, liberated, to your celestial spouse—
To your spouse, in whom alone is found that peace
Which the impious and deceitful world cannot give.
It is a great thing to believe what one does not see,
And greater still to love that from which no sign
Of love toward the lover proceeds,
Which might make the beloved worthy of his love.
And it is a great thing to hope where all faith
Is lacking—that what I seek and plan
I might, according to my primary desire,
Enjoy for a time on earth, and forever in heaven.
And yet, though well overcome by desire,
I think and wish to love my Lord,
And believe and hope in Him, my God,
As much as my unhappy heart is able to do.

Like one who, looking with a more sincere and pure light, clearly sees and discerns the order, the weight, the placement, and the measure <note>This is a reference to the Book of Wisdom 11:20: "But thou hast ordered all things in measure, and number, and weight."</note> of things both visible and eternal; the form and the manner of every creature and their living and eternal beauties; the adornment, the time, the motion, and all that which illuminates the universe and makes it more beautiful.

# On the Abuse and Vanity of Human
# Affairs. Second Frottola.

Thus Fortune turns
O, our human cares,
Blind, foolish, impious, and vain—
Vain, without any fruit.
I have searched the whole world
To see if perhaps in some part,
Sect, profession, or art,
I might find peace.
And behold, everything
Turns out deceptive for me;
Where I thought to pluck the rose,
I find only thorns.

<meta>This page concludes the "Frottola for Pope Leo." The text picks up mid-sentence from the previous page's reference to the Gospel of Luke ("No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back..."), completing the metaphor of the Pope's labor in reforming the Church.</meta>

For your Christian people
Let your pious mantle cover,
At this holy plow <note>A continuation of the biblical metaphor from the previous page (Luke 9:62), suggesting the hard work of spiritual reform and leadership.</note>,
This, your naked bride <term>nuda sposa: the "Naked Bride" is a traditional metaphor for the Church, here portrayed as vulnerable and stripped of her former glory, awaiting restoration by the Pope.</term>.
Until, glorious,
She returns to her first state <note>This refers to the *Ecclesia Primitiva* or the "Primitive Church," an idealized vision of the early Christian community that many Renaissance reformers hoped to recreate.</note>.
Oh, three times blessed,
And even more, my heart, are those
Who, through your gift
And through your grace, O Lord,
Under such a shepherd <note>Referring to Pope Leo X.</note>,
You may bind and gather me.
Wherever Fortune turns
Her wheels as she sees fit,
My heart cannot climb
Because the place is too high.
Now, because for such a great leap
I have but short legs <note>An idiomatic expression of the author's humility and his inability to reach spiritual heights or complete his work without divine aid.</note>,
And because time and death
Press upon me from every side,
To you, Jesus <note>original: "IESV"</note>, I turn
My sighs, tears, and prayers,
So that you might lean down
Through your infinite
Pity, to keep me in life
Long enough that, although unworthy,
I may see your glory and your kingdom on earth.

->THE END.<- <note>original Latin: "FINIS."</note>

<summary>This concluding page of the poem petitions Pope Leo X and Jesus to protect and restore the Church (the "naked bride") to its original purity. The author ends with a humble personal prayer for life and grace to witness the realization of God's kingdom on earth.</summary>
<keywords>Pope Leo X, Bride of Christ, Church reform, Primitive Church, Fortune, Jesus, humility, prayer</keywords>

Burial of the dead on various subjects. 1.
